\chapter{Review --- Second Looks}
\label{ch:repaso-la-superficie}
\hlchaptermodality{319}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can check a Spanish surface against better evidence, name the five stages of a leaving, run an introduction start to finish, and use the five answering words.}

Complete ES-C319-repaso-la-superficie: name the honest witness to a noun's gender, choose between the two sorries, and date the opening question mark.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(review)]{Review — what the surface does not tell you}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-repaso-la-superficie}



\begin{quote}
What does \textbf{pronto} mean on its own? (\textbf{Soon} — and \textquotedblleft{}ready\textquotedblright{}, the sense English kept in \emph{prompt}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four things you met separately, gathered because they share a shape: the part you can see is not the part to trust.

\textbf{First.} \emph{Pronto} is about \textbf{readiness}, from \emph{promptus}; \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{} is where readiness ended up.

\textbf{Second.} \emph{Lo siento} and \emph{perdón} both come out as English \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}. The English does not divide them; the Latin does. One names \textbf{your} feeling, the other asks for \textbf{their} pardon.

\textbf{Third.} \emph{El agua} looks masculine and is not. The article moved for \textbf{sound}; the object pronoun did not, and says \emph{\textbf{la}}.

\textbf{Fourth.} The \emph{h} on \emph{hermano} looks like the \emph{h} on \emph{hijo}. One stood where a Latin \emph{f} was breathed aloud for centuries; the other went on the page long after the sound had gone.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the mark that was designed, not inherited}]
The \textbf{¿} belongs on that list from the other side. It is not a survival: the Spanish Royal Academy made it official in \textbf{1754}, because Spanish leaves the words of a question where they were and something had to warn the reader.

Four inherited surfaces that mislead, and one deliberate surface that helps.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pronto}, then English \emph{prompt}
  \item \emph{el agua}, then \emph{la bebo}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is the honest witness to a noun's gender? (The \textbf{object pronoun}.) When was \textbf{¿} made official? (\textbf{1754}.) Was \emph{hermano}'s \emph{h} ever a sound? (\textbf{No}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the five words of a leaving}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-repaso-salir}



\begin{quote}
Two to start. Say \textquotedblleft{}the street.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{La calle}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}the corner.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{La esquina}}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say the five in order and hear the distance grow at every step: \textbf{la calle}, \textbf{la esquina}, \textbf{la huella}, \textbf{el puerto}, \textbf{el faro} — the street, its corner, the mark left in the dirt, the water's edge, and the light still visible when the town is not.

Now the part worth a second visit. Not one of the five was built for this list. \emph{Calle} was a \textbf{cattle track}, \emph{callis}. \emph{Esquina} is a \textbf{shinbone}, Germanic \emph{skina}. \emph{Huella} comes from a day spent \textbf{treading wool}, \emph{fullāre}. \emph{Puerto} is the Roman \textbf{harbour}, \emph{portus}, twin to the \emph{puerta} on land. And \emph{faro} was an \textbf{island}, Pharos, with a fire on top of a tower.

Five ordinary nouns out of five unrelated quarries. That is the ratio you should expect from here on.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five in order — \emph{la calle}, \emph{la esquina}, \emph{la huella}, \emph{el puerto}, \emph{el faro}
  \item \emph{la puerta}, then \emph{el puerto} — the gate on land, the gate off the sea
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{fullāre}? (\textbf{Treading cloth in a vat} — the trampling that gave \emph{huella} its footprint.) What does \emph{ob portum} describe? (\textbf{A wind standing toward harbour} — an opportunity.) And what is a \emph{faro} in a car park today? (A \textbf{headlight}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the harbour, the light, and see you soon}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-despedida}



\begin{quote}
The last two nouns of the run. Say \textquotedblleft{}the harbour.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{El puerto}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}the lighthouse.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{El faro}}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A leaving needs a \textbf{place} and a \textbf{time}, and you have both.

The place: \textbf{el puerto}, the gate off the sea, and \textbf{el faro}, the light standing at its mouth. The time: \textbf{hasta pronto} — \emph{hasta}, \textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{pronto}, \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}.

Say the whole thing once, slowly, as one leaving:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{El puerto. El faro. Hasta pronto.}
\end{quote}

Three words out of three different centuries and two different languages — a Roman harbour, a Greek island, and an Arabic preposition holding a Latin adjective. You can hear all of that now, which you could not at the start.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el puerto}, \emph{el faro}, \emph{hasta pronto}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two is the light, and which is the water? (\emph{\textbf{El faro}}; \emph{\textbf{el puerto}}.) And what does \emph{pronto} promise? (\textbf{Soon} — you will be back shortly.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — an introduction, start to finish}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-repaso-presentarse}



\begin{quote}
Two to open. Which word is the \textbf{first} name? (\emph{\textbf{El nombre}}.) And which is the family one? (\emph{\textbf{El apellido}}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words, and between them a complete first meeting.

You can name yourself both ways: \textbf{el nombre} and \textbf{el apellido}. You can address the other person: \textbf{señor} or \textbf{señora}, the same Latin \emph{senior} wearing the \emph{-o}/\emph{-a} switch you have used since \emph{bueno} and \emph{buena}. And you can answer the introduction: \textbf{encantado} if you are a man, \textbf{encantada} if you are a woman.

Run it once as one exchange, in your own voice:

\begin{quote}
— Buenos días. Me llamo Ana Ruiz. ¿Cómo se llama usted, \textbf{señor}? — Mi \textbf{nombre} es Luis, y mi \textbf{apellido} es Vargas. \textbf{Encantado}. — \textbf{Encantada}.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el nombre}, then \emph{el apellido}
  \item \emph{señor}, then \emph{señora}
  \item the whole exchange above, both voices
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word is under \emph{señor} and \emph{señora}? (\emph{\textbf{Senior}}.) Which ending does a woman use to answer an introduction? (\textbf{-a} — \emph{encantada}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — two ways to answer an introduction}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-dos-respuestas}



\begin{quote}
What does \textbf{mucho gusto} say, word for word? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Much pleasure\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{gusto} is a taste, and from there a liking.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Somebody has just told you their name. Spanish gives you two answers, and they were minted centuries apart.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you say} & \textbf{it literally means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{mucho gusto} & much pleasure \\
\textbf{encantado} / \textbf{encantada} & put under a spell \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Mucho gusto} is the plain one, and it names a \textbf{feeling}: \emph{gusto} is Latin \emph{gustus}, a taste. \emph{Encantado} is Latin \emph{incantāre}, to sing a spell onto something — English kept it as \textbf{enchanted}, and the raw noun as \textbf{incantation}.

Notice what neither of them does: \textbf{mention the other person}. English says \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet \textbf{you}\textquotedblright{}. Spanish names the pleasure, or names the spell, and leaves you out of it. Either answer is right, and \emph{mucho gusto} never changes its ending while \emph{encantado} agrees with whoever is speaking.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mucho gusto}, then \emph{encantado}
  \item \emph{encantada}, and hear the ending follow the speaker
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which answer changes its ending for the speaker? (\emph{\textbf{Encantado}} / \emph{\textbf{encantada}}.) And which one names a pleasure instead of a spell? (\emph{\textbf{Mucho gusto}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — five answering words, and where they came from}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-repaso-respuestas}



\begin{quote}
Two to open. Which word answers for a \textbf{thing}? (\emph{\textbf{Algo}}.) And which for a \textbf{person}? (\emph{\textbf{Alguien}}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Say the five: \textbf{algo}, \textbf{alguien}, \textbf{nadie}, \textbf{otro}, \textbf{poco}.

Now the part worth a second look. Four of them are built out of two Latin pieces, and once you see the seams the list stops being a list.

\textbf{The \emph{ali-} pair.} \emph{Algo} is \emph{aliquod}, \textquotedblleft{}some other what\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Alguien} is \emph{aliquem}, \textquotedblleft{}some other whom\textquotedblright{}. One for things, one for people — a line Latin drew and Spanish kept exactly. And \emph{otro} is \emph{alter}, the same neighbourhood: Latin's word for the other of \textbf{two}, which is why English \emph{alter}, \emph{alternate} and \emph{alter ego} all carry a pair inside them.

\textbf{The born ones.} \emph{Nadie} is \emph{nati}, \textquotedblleft{}people born\textquotedblright{}, out of \emph{homines nati}. Its twin \emph{nada} was \textquotedblleft{}a thing born\textquotedblright{}. One Latin participle, collapsed twice, into two words for absence.

\textbf{And the fifth.} \emph{Poco} is \emph{paucus}, \textquotedblleft{}few\textquotedblright{} — English \textbf{paucity} straight from the Latin, and English \textbf{few} the same root down the Germanic road after \emph{p} turned to \emph{f}. You already carried \emph{poco} inside \emph{tampoco}, which is \emph{tan} plus \emph{poco}: \textquotedblleft{}so little.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five — \emph{algo}, \emph{alguien}, \emph{nadie}, \emph{otro}, \emph{poco}
  \item \emph{otro}, then \emph{otra}; \emph{poco}, then \emph{poca} — both agree
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many did \emph{alter} mean? (\textbf{Two}.) What is inside \emph{tampoco}? (\emph{\textbf{Tan}} and \emph{\textbf{poco}}.) And what were the \emph{nati} of \emph{nadie}? (\textbf{People born}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the two that agree, and the p that becomes an f}

\label{lesson:ES-C319-otro-y-poco}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}another book,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}another house.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Otro}} libro; \emph{\textbf{otra}} casa.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Of the five answering words, exactly two change their ending: \textbf{otro} and \textbf{poco}. Both are measuring a thing, so both match the thing.

\begin{quote}
\emph{otro} / \emph{otra} — another \emph{poco} / \emph{poca} — a little
\end{quote}

\emph{Algo}, \emph{alguien} and \emph{nadie} never move, because none of them is describing a noun. They \textbf{are} the noun.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\emph{Poco} is Latin \textbf{paucus}, and English \textbf{few} is the same root arriving by the Germanic road, after \emph{p} turned to \emph{f}.

That shift is not a one-off. \emph{Pie} and \textbf{foot}. \emph{Diente} and \textbf{tooth}. \emph{Poco} and \textbf{few}. Three pairs, one sound law — and once you can hear a Spanish \emph{p} behind an English \emph{f}, a large part of English stops looking foreign.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{otro}, \emph{otra}, \emph{poco}, \emph{poca}
  \item \emph{poco} and \emph{few}, then \emph{pie} and \emph{foot}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why do \emph{otro} and \emph{poco} change while \emph{nadie} does not? (They \textbf{describe a noun}; \emph{nadie} is one.) And name the three \emph{p}-to-\emph{f} pairs. (\emph{Pie}/foot, \emph{diente}/tooth, \emph{poco}/few.)
\end{tcolorbox}
